Top Salon Scheduling Software Compared: Features, Pricing and Key Differences Published: 29 Sep 2026 Author: Precedence Research Share: Top Scheduling Software Compared: Head-to-Head Feature Breakdown If you run a salon or a day spa and you are shopping for scheduling software right now, the hard part is not finding options. There are dozens, and most of them will take a booking, send a reminder, and hold a card. The hard part is that the platforms are priced on completely different logic, so two systems that look almost identical on a feature grid can be several thousand dollars apart over a year, depending on how many chairs you have and where your new clients come from. This is a large and growing trade, which is part of why the software market around it is so crowded. Federal labor projections have employment of barbers, hairstylists, and cosmetologists growing 7 percent between 2025 and 2035, off a base of roughly 670,800 jobs. We compared eight platforms that salon and spa owners actually shortlist, and we have written every entry to the same template so the comparison is like-for-like. How This Comparison Was Put Together We started from the pages that currently rank for salon and spa scheduling queries and pulled out every vendor that appeared on more than one of them, then removed the tools that are general-purpose calendar apps with a beauty landing page attached. What was left is the eight platforms below. For each one we did the same three things. We opened the vendor's own pricing page and recorded the published numbers, including per-user charges, per-location charges and card processing rates, because those are the figures that move the annual total. We recorded the current Capterra rating and the review count, as plain text, so you can see how much evidence sits behind each score. Then we identified one limitation for every platform, including the one we placed first. We did not accept "contact us for pricing" as an answer, and no vendor paid for placement or for a particular position in the list. Ratings and prices were checked in September 2026 and they do change, so treat them as a starting point rather than a quote. The Eight Platforms At A Glance Platform Starting price Pricing model Best for Main tradeoff Capterra rating Bookeo $14.95 a month Flat tiers by staff count and booking volume Salons and spas that want a predictable bill Branches run as separate accounts 4.3 (103 reviews) Mangomint $130 a month Base fee plus per user Salons with a front desk and a full service menu High cost floor for very small teams 5.0 (344 reviews) Boulevard $140 a month per location Tiered per location Multi-location salons, spas and medspas Priced per location, entry tier caps professionals 4.6 (389 reviews) GlossGenius $24 a month Flat tiers, payments included Solo stylists and small teams Rooms, waivers and waitlist sit on higher tiers 4.8 (349 reviews) Fresha $19.95 a month Subscription plus new-client commission Salons that want marketplace demand 20 percent commission on new marketplace clients 4.8 (1,447 reviews) Vagaro $30 a month Scales with bookable calendars Mixed beauty and wellness businesses Marketing tools and branded app excluded from trial 4.7 (3,651 reviews) Square Appointments $0 a month Free tier, then per location Salons already on Square hardware No-show fees and waitlist require a paid plan 4.5 (260 reviews) Acuity Scheduling $16 a month Tiered by number of calendars Single-service providers and small studios A scheduler rather than a salon system 4.8 (5,758 reviews) 1. Bookeo Best for: salons and spas that want a predictable flat monthly bill and industry-specific scheduling rather than a percentage of every booking. If you are comparing these eight platforms on cost, this is the one where the pricing structure is the main argument. Bookeo prices on staff count and on monthly booking volume, so the bill does not move when you have a good month, and the software vendor does not take a commission out of a booking; card processing runs through Stripe, Square, or PayPal at those providers' own published rates. The appointments product is also one of three separate products (the other two are built for classes and for tours and activities), which is a different design decision from the single general-purpose system that most of this category ships. Key features Real-time booking through a widget embedded in your existing site, or a standalone branded booking page if you do not have one

Staff assigned to specific services with working hours set per staff member and per location, plus calendar sync with Google Calendar, iCal, Outlook and Office 365

Deposits, full prepayment or a card held on file, with automatic email and text reminders and online rescheduling

Client database with intake forms, prepaid packages, memberships and gift vouchers, and digital waivers as a paid add-on Pricing: five tiers, quoted on the US pricing page as Solo at $14.95, Small at $29.95, Standard at $39.95, Large at $79.95, and X-Large at $119.95 a month. The tiers run from 1 consultant and 200 bookings a month up to 60 consultants and 3,000 bookings a month. Digital waivers are an add-on at $9 to $249 a month depending on volume, and text credits are $0.09 each. The free trial is 30 days with no credit card required. Rating: 4.3 on Capterra from 103 reviews. Where it falls short: multi-branch businesses are handled through a portal in which customers search for a branch or centre and then book with that individual branch, and each branch is a standalone account that controls its own schedule, staff, customer database, sales reports and statistics. Data is not shared between branches. Each branch has its own customers, its own members and its own gift vouchers, so a voucher bought at one branch can only be redeemed at that branch. The portal manager can go into each sub-account's backend and pull portal reports (booking summaries and a revenue summary) for each sub-account, but if you are expecting one combined customer list across five sites, that is not the model. The review base is also small next to the platforms further down this list, which is worth knowing when you are reading scores. 2. Mangomint Best for: salons and spas with a front desk and a full-service menu that want one system running the floor rather than a calendar and a till kept separately. Mangomint is built on the assumption that you have a front desk and somebody standing at it. Pricing is $120 a month as a base fee plus $10 per user, so the smallest realistic monthly bill is $130, and the bill rises with headcount rather than with bookings. What you get for that is a system intended to run the whole floor rather than only the calendar, which includes point of sale, retail and inventory, forms and charting, and staff management. Key features Calendar, online booking, Express Booking and a virtual waiting room for walk-ins and gaps

Point of sale with retail and inventory, gift cards, memberships and packages

Forms and charting, client management and web chat

Staff management, reporting and multi-location support in the base plan Pricing: $120 a month base plus $10 per user, with additional locations at $120 a month each. Add-ons are priced separately, including phone at $70 a month per line, marketing from $30 a month, and payroll at $50 a month plus $8 per worker. Card processing is 2.45 percent plus 15 cents in person and 2.90 percent plus 30 cents for virtual transactions. A free trial account is available. Rating: 5.0 on Capterra from 344 reviews. Where it falls short: the cost floor. A three-stylist salon is at $150 a month before a single add-on, and a solo operator is paying for a front-desk system that will not be used. The reporting and inventory depth is real, but it is depth you have to be big enough to need. 3. Boulevard Best for: multi-location salons, spas and medspas that need per-location control, per-location reporting and treatment-side depth. Boulevard is priced and reported per location, and that is the design assumption underneath the whole product rather than an option that has been added on afterwards. The tiers escalate on the number of professionals and on the volume of texts and email blasts included. It appears on medspa shortlists about as often as it appears on salon shortlists, which is a reasonable signal about where the product depth actually sits. Key features Per-location scheduling, reporting, and staff permissions

Client messaging with included text and email allowances that scale by tier

Forms as a paid add-on for intake and consent, which matters for treatment-led businesses

Integrations including QuickBooks as a paid add-on Pricing: Essentials is $176 a month per location, or $140 with annual billing, and covers up to 5 professionals with 100 texts, 500 email blasts, and 25 GB of storage. Premier is $293, or $234 annually, and lifts that to unlimited professionals, 250 texts, and 1,000 email blasts. Prestige is $410, or $328 annually, and adds the forms add-on with 2,500 texts and 10,000 email blasts. Enterprise pricing is quoted on request. Forms is $65 a month; QuickBooks is $45 a month. Rating: 4.6 on Capterra from 389 reviews. Where it falls short: the price. Two locations on Essentials is $280 a month at least, and the entry tier stops at 5 professionals, which many two-site salons will pass quickly. Card processing rates are not published on the pricing page, so you will have to ask for them before you can compare the real cost against the platforms that do publish. 4. GlossGenius Best for: solo stylists and small teams that want one flat price with card processing included in it. Solo stylists and small teams are the audience here, and the pricing reflects that. The Standard plan is $24 a month billed annually and includes the booking site, client notifications, email and text marketing, inventory and retail, and packages and memberships, with card processing at a flat 2.6 percent. For a one-chair business, that is a straightforward number to plan against. Key features Custom booking website with unlimited client notifications

Email and text marketing included from the entry plan

Inventory, retail, packages and memberships

Forms and waivers, Google booking, automated waitlist, and room and resource management from the Gold plan Pricing: Standard is $24 a month, Gold is $48 a month, and Platinum is $148 a month, all billed annually. Medspa plans are separate at $148 and $248 a month. Card processing is a flat 2.6 percent with no extra charge for tap-to-pay or card on file; instant payouts cost 1.8 percent, and the payroll add-on is $40 a month plus $6 a seat. The free trial is 14 days with no credit card. Rating: 4.8 on Capterra from 349 reviews. Where it falls short: the features a spa needs are not on the cheap plan. Room and resource management, automated waitlist, and forms and waivers all start on Gold at $48 a month, which is double the headline price. If you are a hair salon, the Standard plan may well be enough; if you have treatment rooms, it probably is not. 5. Fresha Best for: salons that want marketplace demand and are willing to pay a commission for the new clients that marketplace sends them. With Fresha, the subscription price is not the figure that decides what you pay in a year. Fresha charges $19.95 a month for an independent professional and $14.95 per team member per month for a team, which is genuinely low, and it then takes a 20 percent one-time commission on every new client who books through the Fresha marketplace, with a minimum fee of $6 per client, while returning clients are free. That commission is a customer acquisition channel with a price attached to it, and our view is that it gets misread as free software more often than any other pricing arrangement in this category. Key features Marketplace exposure to consumers searching for salons in your area

Subscription priced per team member rather than per location

Card processing built in, with buy now pay later available through Klarna

Optional add-ons for loyalty, insights, review generation, and an AI concierge Pricing: Independent is $19.95 a month, Team is $14.95 per team member a month, and enterprise pricing is quoted on request. The new-client marketplace commission is 20 percent with a $6 minimum per client. Online card payments are 2.79 percent plus $0.20; in-person payments are 2.29 percent plus $0.20 with an extra 10 cents for tap-to-pay, and manual card entry is 3.30 percent plus $0.20. Add-ons include client loyalty at $59.95 a month per location, insights at $9.95 per bookable team member, and an AI concierge at $99.95 a month per location. Rating: 4.8 on Capterra from 1,447 reviews. Where it falls short: the commission is charged on new clients, which means the cost of the platform rises exactly when the business is growing. If most of your new bookings already come from your own site, your own social accounts or word of mouth, you are paying a marketplace rate for demand you generated yourself, and you should model that before you switch. 6. Vagaro Best for: mixed beauty and wellness businesses where several different kinds of providers share one roof and one booking system. Vagaro has been in this market a long time, and it shows in the breadth of the feature list and in the size of the review base, which is over 3,600 on Capterra. The entry price is low and the platform scales by the number of bookable calendars rather than by location, which suits mixed businesses where hair, nails, massage and fitness share a roof. Key features Booking, calendars and client records for beauty, wellness and fitness businesses in one system

Website builder, marketing tools and a branded client app available in the subscription

Merchant services with a card reader included on sign-up

Pricing tiers selected by the number of bookable calendars, from one up to seven or more Pricing: the published rate is $23.99 a month as an introductory price for the first six months, with a standard price of $30.00, and the plan cost rises as you add bookable calendars. The free trial is 30 days and covers all features except email marketing, text marketing and the branded app. Card processing rates are quoted through Vagaro merchant services rather than published on the pricing page. Rating: 4.7 on Capterra from 3,651 reviews. Where it falls short: the trial excludes email marketing, text marketing and the branded app, which are three of the things a salon is most likely to be evaluating. You can trial the calendar but not the growth tools, so the first real test of those happens after you are already paying. 7. Square Appointments Best for: salons that already take payment on Square hardware and want the booking calendar attached to the till. There is a free tier here, and for a solo stylist who already takes payments on Square hardware it is a reasonable place to start, because booking is attached to the till and the reporting is one system rather than two. The paid tiers are priced per location and they also buy down the card processing rate, which is unusual and worth doing the arithmetic on if your card volume is high. Key features Online booking site, integrations, appointment reminders and unlimited staff calendars on the free plan

Cancellation policy, no-show fees, multi-staff appointment booking and a waitlist on the Plus plan

Future bookings report, service cost tracking and resource management on the Premium plan

Booking, payments, and reporting in one account with Square point of sale Pricing: Square Free is $0 a month, Square Plus is $49 a month per location, and Square Premium is $149 a month per location. In-person card processing is 2.6 percent plus 15 cents on Free, 2.5 percent plus 15 cents on Plus, and 2.4 percent plus 15 cents on Premium. Online payments are 3.3 percent plus 30 cents on Free and 2.9 percent plus 30 cents on the paid plans. Paid plans include a trial period. Rating: 4.5 on Capterra from 260 reviews. Where it falls short: the free plan is thin in the places where salons actually lose money. Cancellation policies, no-show fees, and the waitlist all require Plus at $49 a month per location. Payment processing is also Square-only, so if you have a processing rate you like elsewhere, you cannot bring it with you. 8. Acuity Scheduling Best for: single-service providers, mobile therapists, and small studios that need a scheduler rather than a salon management system. Acuity Scheduling is a scheduling tool that a lot of beauty professionals use, rather than a salon management system that happens to schedule. It is owned by Squarespace; the calendar and intake side is well built, and it is priced by the number of calendars you need rather than by staff or by location. For a single-service provider, a small studio or a mobile therapist, that is often the right shape. Key features Client self-scheduling with unlimited services and appointments on every plan

Payments through Stripe, Square, PayPal, and Venmo

SMS reminders, packages, and gift certificates from the Standard plan

HIPAA business associate agreement and custom API and CSS access on Premium Pricing: Starter is $16 a month billed annually or $20 monthly and includes 1 calendar. Standard is $27 annually or $34 monthly and includes up to 6 calendars. Premium is $49 annually or $61 monthly and includes up to 36 calendars. The free trial is 7 days and does not require a credit card. Rating: 4.8 on Capterra from 5,758 reviews. Where it falls short: it is a scheduler, and the salon-specific layer is not the centre of the product. There is no retail-first design, and the trial is only 7 days, which is short if you intend to import a client list, build a service menu, and test a real week of bookings before you decide. What to compare besides the booking calendar Most feature grids in this category compare the same eight things, and most of those eight are now table stakes. These are the areas where the platforms above genuinely differ. Online booking and per-staff calendars Every platform here will publish availability and take a booking. What varies is whether the system understands that a service is tied to a specific person with specific hours, that some services can only be performed by some staff, and that two stylists cannot occupy the same station. If you have more than two people, ask to see double-booking prevention configured, not described. Deposits, Cancellation Windows and No-Show Fees This is the group of settings that has money directly attached to it, and it is the group where the detail is worth checking carefully. A workable configuration will let you require a deposit or full prepayment on selected services, hold a card on file for the rest, define a cancellation window, and then charge the fee automatically when somebody cancels inside that window. Note that once you store a card to charge a late-cancellation fee later, you are handling payment account data. The standards for that are set by the card industry's security council, which was founded in 2006 by the major payment brands, and compliance is a question you should be asking your software vendor rather than assuming. Client Self-Service: Rescheduling, Cancelling And The Waitlist Self-service is the feature that removes phone calls, and it has two halves. The first is that a client can move or cancel a booking from the confirmation email or a client area without calling the salon. The second is that when a slot is released, the system automatically offers it to a waitlist rather than leaving a hole in the day. Plenty of platforms do the first. Fewer do the second, and on some of them the automated waitlist sits on a higher tier, so check which plan it is on before you price the system. Memberships, Packages And Gift Vouchers If you sell a six-session package or a monthly membership, the software has to track the balance, the expiry and the recurring charge, and it has to do that at the point of booking rather than in a spreadsheet afterwards. Gift vouchers are a separate question again, particularly for multi-site businesses, because the rules about where a voucher can be redeemed differ by platform. The Layer Beyond Booking: Point Of Sale, Retail And Staff Commission For a hair salon with a retail shelf and a commission structure, the booking calendar is maybe half the job. Point of sale, inventory, and commission tracking on both services and product sales are the parts that decide whether you are running one system or three. Mangomint and Boulevard are built with that layer in mind; the lower-priced schedulers generally are not, and that is a fair reason for the price gap. Client Apps And Staff Apps These are two different things, and they get conflated. A client app is a booking app your customers install, and it is mostly a retention and rebooking tool. A staff app is what your team uses to see their own schedule, check a client note before a service, and take a payment on the floor. Some vendors charge for one or the other, and a branded client app is frequently an add-on rather than an inclusion. Integrations The list to check is short and specific: your calendar (Google, Outlook, iCal or Office 365), your payment processor, your accounting package, and your email marketing tool. If a platform forces its own payment processing, that is not automatically bad, but it does mean the card rate is part of the subscription decision rather than separate from it. The Pricing Model, Which Is Where Most Of The Money Is Three models are in use across the eight platforms above, and they behave very differently as a business grows. A flat tier priced on staff count and booking volume is predictable, and it does not cost you more in a month when trade is good. The second model, a base fee plus a per-user charge, is manageable at three people and gets expensive at twelve, because the per-user line is charged whether or not that person is generating bookings. The third model, a commission on new clients, is inexpensive while you are quiet and increasingly expensive while you are growing, which is the opposite of what most owners assume when they sign up. Salons are small businesses in the statistical sense as well as the everyday one, since by the federal government's own count 99.9 percent of businesses are small, and at that scale a $10 per-user line item is not a rounding error. Build the twelve-month total under each model with your real numbers before you compare feature lists. Solo, Single-Site Or Multi-Location Changes The Answer For a solo stylist or a single mobile therapist, the calendar is the product, and almost everything else is overhead. GlossGenius, Acuity Scheduling, and the free Square Appointments tier all make sense at that size, and paying $130 a month for inventory and payroll you do not use is a poor trade. For a single location with three to ten staff, the decision usually comes down to whether you need the retail and commission layer. If you do, Mangomint and Boulevard are the serious candidates and the cost is justified. If you do not, a flat-tier platform such as Bookeo or a per-calendar platform such as Vagaro will cover the same booking workload for a fraction of the monthly cost. For multi-location businesses, ask one blunt question early: what exactly is shared between sites, and what is not. Some platforms give you one account with several locations inside it and consolidated reporting. Others, including Bookeo with its portal model, run each branch as a separate account with its own customers, staff, reports and vouchers, and give the portal manager access to each sub-account plus per-sub-account portal reports rather than a merged view. Neither approach is wrong. A franchise where each branch is independently owned often prefers the separated model, while a three-site group under one owner usually wants the consolidated one. What causes trouble is buying the first when you assumed the second, so get the vendor to demonstrate it on your own structure before you sign anything. Which One To Pick Naming one overall winner here would be tidy, and it would also be wrong, because the eight platforms are aimed at businesses of quite different sizes. Mangomint and Boulevard are the strongest choices when the business is large enough to need the full operations layer and can carry the monthly cost of it. For solo operators and very small teams, GlossGenius, Acuity Scheduling and the free Square Appointments tier are all sensible starting points. Fresha is a good arrangement if the marketplace is genuinely bringing you clients you would not otherwise have had, and a poor one if it is not, so that is the number to check first. Vagaro sits in the middle and tends to suit mixed beauty and wellness businesses that have several kinds of providers under one roof. If what you want is salon scheduling software with a predictable flat monthly cost, industry-specific booking rather than a general calendar tool, and no commission taken out of your bookings, Bookeo is built for that buyer, with the caveat about branch separation noted above. Whichever way you go, work out the twelve-month total under each pricing model using your own staff count and your own new-client numbers before you compare anything else. The feature lists across these eight platforms are fairly similar to one another. The annual invoices are not.

Lumin Digital and Community Financial Services Bank among 100 best medium workplaces of 2026
Lumin Digital, Community Financial Services Bank and PeopleTec have been named as some of the 100 best medium workplaces of 2026.
To determine the 100 best small and medium workplaces of 2026, Fortune partnered with global people analytics firm Great Place to Work to analyse survey feedback representing US employees.
To be eligible for the best medium workplaces list, firms must be Great Place To Work certified and must have between 100 and 999 employees. For the best small workplaces list, organisations also need to be Great Place To Work certified and have between 10 and 99 workers.
A majority (96%) of employees at the best medium workplaces said their firm was a great place to work, 37% more than the average at a typical workplace of the same size. For those at the best small workplaces, the average was 98%.

- Lumin Digital
- Home Genius Exteriors
- Westpac Wealth Partners
- PeopleTec
- Community Financial Services Bank
The top five best small workplaces are:
- 5

- Mangomint
- Proper Roofing and Remodeling
A Great Place to Work spokesperson said: “Employees tell us whether leaders are accessible, communicate honestly and clearly, and if their actions match their words. They tell us whether they feel respected as individuals, if they receive training benefits, appreciation, support for their wellbeing and opportunities to contribute. They tell us whether they believe their firm is fair related to pay, profits, promotions, recognition and opportunities. They tell us if they are proud of their work, their team, and their firm and if they feel they make a difference, and their work is meaningful. And they tell us whether they enjoy the people they work with, feel cared for and can be themselves.
“List rankings are based on this feedback, which we analyse to determine the extent to which this experience is shared by the full workforce. We identify the organisations that offer the most generous, caring and innovative cultures reflecting a genuine commitment to meet the diversity of their people’s needs inside and outside the workplace.”

Staff Writer ・ Editorial Read Staff 's Posts August 3, 2026 Mangomint simplifies its pricing model, making more features available without an upgrade. Credit : Mangomint 2 min to read Share Mangomint introduces a new pricing model that simplifies costs for its users.

Customers can now access premium features without needing to upgrade their plans. *Summarized by AI Mangomint is rolling out a new, simplified pricing model that moves in the opposite direction of where most software companies are headed: instead of new tiers, upcharges, or feature paywalls, the salon and spa software platform is lowering costs and giving all customers access to features that used to require an upgrade. Starting August 1, 2026, every Mangomint customer moves to one plan: $120/month per location plus $10/month per user. “Mangomint is a premium platform, and we’d set the price accordingly. With this change, our goal is to make the same premium platform and service accessible to literally all salons and spas,” says Daniel Lang, CEO at Mangomint. More Tools Included Mangomint's core features that previously required an upgrade are now available to all Mangomint customers at no additional cost: -Express Booking -Memberships -Virtual Waiting Room -Forms & Charting -Web Chat -HIPAA compliance (with a signed BAA) -Integrations, including Shopify and Webhooks Optional add-ons remain for salons and spas that need them—phone (calls and texting), full-service payroll, and marketing—but the core of the platform is now available to every customer, not gated behind the pricier plans. Redefining the Standard for Salon and Spa Software The move lands at a moment when many companies, across nearly every industry, are raising prices and gutting access. Mangomint's approach is a deliberate bet that simplicity and inclusion, not segmentation, is what salon and spa owners want from their software partner. “The goal is to remove the pricing barrier for businesses that could really benefit from Mangomint today,” says Iris Pyland, Mangomint’s VP of Customer Operations. “We want to make it easy for them to get started on day one, and then help them grow with Mangomint.” Existing Mangomint customers don't need to do anything to make the switch—it happens automatically on August 1. Mangomint says any customer whose bill would have gone up under the new structure will be grandfathered at their current price. About Mangomint: Mangomint is an all-in-one business management platform built for salons, spas, and other beauty businesses. The platform combines scheduling, payments, client management, marketing, and staff management tools designed to help beauty and wellness businesses run more efficiently and grow. Business Tips FAQ: Everything You Need to Know About Salon Software in 2026 by Booksy Team

Choosing the right technology is the most important business decision a salon owner in the digital age can make. With so many options on the market, from specialized booking apps to massive enterprise systems, it’s easy to feel overwhelmed. This FAQ guide answers the most common questions about salon software features, pricing, and functionality to help you find the perfect fit for your business goals. What is the best salon software? The "best" software depends on your salon's size and needs. Booksy Biz is widely considered the top all-in-one choice due to its balance of powerful marketing tools and an intuitive mobile experience. Other industry leaders include Vagaro (great for multi-service hubs), Mangomint (known for its clean design), and Phorest (strong for established brands). Which salon software has built-in loyalty features? Booksy Biz offers one of the most effective digital stamp card and points systems for loyal customers. Other platforms with dedicated loyalty modules include Phorest (with their "TreatCard" system), Zenoti, and Vagaro. Which salon software has the best reporting features? For deep data analysis, Booksy Biz provides excellent real-time insights into revenue and staff performance. 5 Honest Lessons on How AI is Actually Rewiring B2B Sales (From Salesforce, Momentum, and Mangomint)

We put three very different revenue leaders on stage at SaaStr AI London: Greg Beltzer CCO of Salesforce Agentforce (former CIO), Ashley Wilson COO and co-founder Momentum (AI-native B2B company), and Marchelle Mooney from Mangomint (VP of Sales running a very SMB vertical B2B org selling to salons and spas). They had wildly different contexts. Salesforce has tens of thousands of sellers. Momentum is a 50-person AI startup. Mangomint’s AEs close 20 logos a month at SMB ACVs. But they kept arriving at the same conclusions. Here’s what actually matters right now. 1. Your AI Rollout Will Be Bumpy. That’s Normal. Greg was blunt about this: the Agentforce rollout at Salesforce itself has not been smooth. Data wasn’t clean. Processes weren’t ready. Ways of working had to be rewritten on the fly. This is Salesforce we’re talking about. The CRM company. If their data wasn’t in a perfect place for AI, yours probably isn’t either. The key insight from Greg: AI is much easier to deploy on the service and ops side than on the sales side. Why? Because service and support workflows already have structured data and defined processes. You’re already doing those activities with humans in a documented way. Sales is different. You’re relying on individual sellers, and most of what they know lives in their heads, their text messages, or nowhere at all. If you’re starting your AI journey, start where your data is cleanest. For most companies, that’s support or operations, not sales. 2. Every Company Has Leads They Never Followed Up With. AI Fixes This Immediately. This was the single biggest “everyone in the room nodded” moment. Greg admitted that Salesforce gets a massive volume of inbound web leads and a shockingly low percentage were being followed up on. Reps cherry-picked the ones they wanted. The rest got a fake loss reason with no notes in the record. Sound familiar? Amelia SaaStr’s Chief AI Officer shared the same experience at SaaStr AI: post-Annual, hundreds of leads from people who literally raised their hand to sponsor, and the sales team just… didn’t call them. Not because they’re bad people. Because humans prioritize, and the bottom 40% of leads always gets ignored. This is the single easiest AI use case in sales right now. Put an agent on the leads nobody is working. Not because the agent is going to close a $50K deal. But because it will follow up consistently, enrich the data, qualify or disqualify, and surface the ones worth a human’s time. Greg’s number: the leads worked by agents at Salesforce led to direct revenue they would not have had otherwise, because nobody was working those leads at all. If you do nothing else with AI in sales this year, do this. 3. Your CRM Data Is Worse Than You Think, and AI Will Show You Marchelle had the most honest take on this. When she started rolling out Momentum and other AI tools, she realized her Salesforce instance was a mess. Deals were closed with no notes. No call logs. No contact records. Her marketing automation platform had 10,000 more data points than Salesforce, even though Salesforce should have had more (since it gets both marketing and sales data pushed into it). Her top rep was closing 35 logos a month. Absolute machine. But everything lived in text messages. No notes in the CRM. Another rep literally had to explain to his wife why he had so many women in his text messages because he’d never sold to salon and spa owners before. These are real humans doing real things that don’t show up in your system of record. Here’s the problem: if data never existed as a record in your CRM, your AI agent can’t go back and find it. It’s not going to magically reconstruct what happened. So the first step for many teams isn’t deploying an agent. It’s deploying tools (like Momentum, Gong, or whatever fits your stack) that ensure data actually makes it into Salesforce going forward. Marchelle’s advice: pick your AI tools based on what will ensure everything flows back to one source of truth. Then build agents on top of clean data. 4. Don’t Raise Quota Yet. Use AI to Lift Your Middle Performers. Marchelle announced to her team that she is not raising quota in 2026. She could have. Her top performers are closing 35 logos a month against a 20-logo quota. That’s a 7x ARR-to-OTE ratio in very SMB SaaS. But she chose a different strategy: keep quota flat and use AI to push the middle of the bell curve up toward top-performer levels. Her logic is sound. We’re not at the point where AI is truly native in most sales workflows. If you raise quota now, you’re asking reps to do more before you’ve actually given them the systems to do more. You’ll just create frustration. Ashley reinforced this from her research for a report Momentum published. Multiple revenue leaders, including Kyle Norton at Owner.com, said the same thing: the companies winning with AI in sales are investing heavily in ops and rev ops headcount to run agents, manage data, and architect systems from top of funnel through post-sales. The efficiency gains only happen if the business supports the reps with all the underlying infrastructure. Ashley’s direct quote on the “two reps to $100M” narrative: sure, that works if you’re Lovable. But most of us don’t have that business. Holding yourself to that standard is unrealistic. Better to invest in the systems that will compound over time. One exception: if you’re an AI-native startup and everyone is already crushing a low quota, you probably have the wrong quota. One founder Ashley spoke with had a head of sales running the “industry standard playbook” at a company where every rep was hitting quota easily. That’s not a sign of a great team. That’s a sign the bar is too low. First principles matter more than borrowed playbooks. 5. AI for Customer Retention Is the Underrated Play Most companies are focused on AI for top-of-funnel or support chatbots. Almost nobody is using AI seriously for retention. Ashley thinks that’s a mistake. Customer success teams have been underserved in tooling for years. The expectation is still high on them to get data into Salesforce or Gainsight, but the tools haven’t matched the ask. Meanwhile, churn is usually a slow drip, not a sudden event. A customer doesn’t wake up one day and leave. They have three unanswered support tickets, a feature request that went nowhere, and a quiet conversation where they mentioned they’re “evaluating options.” With AI listening to those calls and flagging dissatisfaction signals in real time, CS leaders can actually intervene before the renewal conversation turns into a save attempt. Ashley shared an example: a customer doing 3-hour support calls in another language, then having to manually write notes into Salesforce. Now that’s automated, translated, and searchable. The time savings alone change what’s possible for a CSM’s book of business. Greg added context from financial services: 40% of customers want more outreach from their vendors, but they want it to be relevant and personalized, not a drip campaign. That’s exactly what an agent can do. It builds the relationship digitally, one small interaction at a time, so the human can close it when it matters. A Few More Quick Takeaways From the Panel AI is easier to sell into organizations than it was two years ago, but internal resistance from legal, CIOs, and works councils is still the #1 blocker. You need a champion inside the company raising the flag. It doesn’t happen by just giving people a Claude license.

You need a champion inside the company raising the flag. It doesn’t happen by just giving people a Claude license. Your top seller will never put notes in the CRM. Stop fighting it. Deploy tools that capture the data automaticall y. The personality type that closes 35 deals a month is not the personality type that writes call summaries.

The personality type that closes 35 deals a month is not the personality type that writes call summaries. AI-generated outbound sequences work, but video messages on LinkedIn still break through the noise better than anything automated . Ashley’s team in Argentina uses AI to write sequences, but the human-recorded videos are what actually get responses.

Ashley’s team in Argentina uses AI to write sequences, but the human-recorded videos are what actually get responses. If your marketing automation platform has more data than your CRM, something is broken . Marshelle found hers were nearly even when Salesforce should have had significantly more. That gap is your AI ceiling.

Marshelle found hers were nearly even when Salesforce should have had significantly more. That gap is your AI ceiling. CS is where AI might have the biggest retention impact, but almost nobody is deploying there yet . Churn is a slow drip of unanswered signals. AI that listens for dissatisfaction in real time catches what CSMs with 50-account books can’t. No One’s Replacing Sellers with AI. Not Yet At Least. None of these leaders talked about replacing humans with AI. Every single one of them talked about fixing the basics that humans never did well in the first place: following up on every lead, keeping clean CRM data, reaching out to customers post-sale, and giving reps the systems to spend more time selling. The companies that will pull ahead aren’t the ones with the fanciest agents. They’re the ones that got their data right, deployed AI on the unsexy problems first, and invested in the operational infrastructure to make it all work. Start with the leads no one is working. Get your data into one source of truth. Don’t raise quota until you’ve earned the right to. And for the love of everything, use AI for retention before your customers quietly walk out the door. What Every B2B Founder Needs to Know About AI in Go-To-Market Right Now With Jason Lemkin

The State of AI + Software: Where It’s Going – Fast This deep dive is from Jason Lemkin at the LIVE AI Workshop Wednesday. Sign up here for the next one. I was talking to a founder recently who’s running at $50 million ARR. Classic SaaS guy turned AI guy. And he’s going to scale from $50M to $100M with just five sales reps and a team of AI agents. In the old days, at $50 million, you’d probably have at least 100 sales reps. Why? Because to get from $50M to $100M, you need $50M in net new bookings. At $500K net per rep (which is pretty good when you factor in scaling, turnover, and ramp time), you’d need 100 bodies. Minimum. This founder? Five human reps. Plus AI. It’s not that he doesn’t need sales reps. It’s not even that he’s not selling. He’s actually doing classic B2B SaaS sales. He’s just doing it with dramatically fewer humans, and for the purposes of this discussion, he’s doing it so much more efficiently. And he has 10,000+ inbound leads a month flowing through this system. This is where we are right now. And if you’re not paying attention, you’re already behind. Everything Changed For SaaStr Itself in the Last 180 Days At the end of Q1 this year, we had zero AI agents in production at SaaStr. Nothing. Nada. We were thinking about it, but we hadn’t deployed anything. Fast forward to today, and we’ve got: Almost 20 AI agents running in production

Four different AI SDRs deployed and actively working leads

Salesforce Agent Force rolled out (just started yesterday, so we need a bit more time before sharing all the data)

An AI BDR from Qualified handling inbound qualification

A slew of specialized agents for support, research, and operations It is so much different even on our little team than it was even 100 days ago. And it’s going to keep changing at this pace. I’ll be honest: we were probably a little behind the curve at the start of the year. Now, we’re kind of at the bleeding edge. And we want to drag everybody along with us because everything’s changing. The models are changing. The tools are changing. Things that didn’t work last year can work really well now. Everyone complained about how crummy AI SDRs were last year—and there still are a lot of issues—but now we know how to train them. Now we know how to iterate with them. Now we know how to make them work. There’s so much more coming, and marketing in some ways is even further behind sales. But it won’t be for long. This whole space is going to radically change in the next 12 months. More on our AI Agents here. The Single Most Important Thing You Need to Do to Stay Relevant Here’s my advice, and I mean this with every fiber of my being: If you feel behind in AI and go-to-market, the answer is simple: be part of a deployment. Not just “buy a tool and forget about it.” That teaches you absolutely nothing. Go buy any tool. Go buy any tool that comes and talks at events. Go buy any leading tool in the space. At some level, it doesn’t even matter which one you start with. But here’s the critical part: Don’t just buy it. Be part of the deployment. Train it yourself

Be part of the onboarding

Be part of the errors and the issues

Be part of the daily iterations you have to do to get it working Don’t just set and forget. You will learn nothing. You will learn absolutely nothing. Be part of a deployment to see how it really works. Otherwise, you’ll never really learn. You don’t have to become a vibe coder like I have. You don’t even need to play with the underlying tech. What you really need to do is get your hands dirty with actual implementation. The Iconiq Growth Report: 10 Things That Show How Much the World Is Changing Iconiq Growth—one of the top late-stage B2B growth funds forever, from the early days when they managed Mark Zuckerberg’s family money to being in so many leaders from Canva to Anthropic and beyond—just put out an incredible report. Iconiq’s State of Software in 2025: Forward Deployed Engineers Up 12x; 55% of GTM is Now in Post-Sales; 2025 Is Crushing 2024 For Funding It’s almost 100 pages. There’s a lot of detail in there about public companies and nuances that a lot of you don’t really care about. But I picked out what I think are the 10 most relevant things to SaaS folks for B2B that show just how much the world is changing. A lot of folks are behind here. A lot of folks. And it’s okay—it’s not necessarily fatal. We’re not all being killed by ChatGPT and Anthropic. But the world is changing. This data shows you just how it’s changing and how we all have to adapt. 1. AI Native Companies Are Burning Less (Way Less) This first data point explains a lot of things that are really confusing on social media. People say, “Oh, these AI native companies, they’re burning all this cash to acquire customers with free tiers and consumption models.” Actually? Not true. AI native companies burn substantially less than classic SaaS companies did at the same stage. Why? Because they don’t need to hire armies of people to scale. The unit economics work differently when AI is doing a significant portion of the work. 2. The Sales Team Size Cliff We’re seeing companies hit $10M, $25M, even $50M ARR with radically smaller sales teams than the old playbook required. The old rule of thumb: you needed roughly one sales rep per $500K-$1M in ARR, depending on your ACV and sales cycle. The new reality: AI-native companies are operating with 20-30% of the headcount at equivalent revenue levels. That $50M company I mentioned at the beginning? That’s not an outlier. That’s the new normal for AI-native companies. 3. CAC Payback Periods Are Compressing Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC) payback periods are getting shorter in AI-native companies. Not because they’re spending less on acquisition (though some are), but because they’re able to onboard, activate, and expand customers faster with AI-powered customer success and product experiences. We’re seeing companies hit CAC payback in 6-8 months that would have taken 12-18 months in the classic SaaS playbook. 4. Net Revenue Retention Is Under Pressure Everywhere Here’s the uncomfortable truth: Net Revenue Retention (NRR) is declining across the board. Even the best SaaS companies are seeing NRR pressure. Why? Competition is fiercer than ever

Customers are more price-sensitive post-2021

AI is enabling customers to do more with less, reducing expansion

New AI-native alternatives are constantly emerging The days of 130%+ NRR being table stakes? Those are largely over. Now, 120% is excellent. 115% is solid. And anything above 110% in the current environment is worth celebrating. 5. The Growth Multiple Advantage of AI Companies Here’s where it gets really interesting: AI companies are trading at higher multiples than pure SaaS companies at equivalent growth rates. Why? Because investors believe: The TAM is larger (AI can address bigger markets)

The margin structure is better long-term

The defensibility is stronger (data moats, model improvements)

The growth trajectory is more durable A SaaS company growing 100% YoY might trade at 10-15x ARR. An AI company growing 100% YoY? We’re seeing 20-30x+ ARR in some cases. 6. Time to $10M ARR Is Accelerating AI-native companies are hitting $10M ARR significantly faster than classic SaaS companies did. Classic SaaS: 3-5 years from founding to $10M ARR was typical for fast-growing companies. AI-native: We’re seeing companies hit $10M ARR in 18-24 months. Why? Product-led growth combined with AI efficiency. Lower go-to-market costs. Faster time to value. Viral distribution. 7. The Disappearance of the Middle-Market Private Equity Exit This one is painful but important: The private equity exit path for $20M-$50M ARR SaaS companies has essentially disappeared. In the 2010s and early 2020s, if you had a solid SaaS company growing 30-50%, your burn rate was low, and your NRR was high, maybe VCs wouldn’t touch you, but a private equity firm would come in and buy you for 6x to sometimes 10x revenue. You’d get to $20M revenue growing 50-60% and cash flow neutral. No VC was going to fund you there, but a PE firm might buy you for $150M or even $200M. I don’t see any of those deals anymore. They’ve disappeared. Why? Because private equity isn’t immune to the fact that: Public SaaS companies have seen growth decay

NRR isn’t as sticky as it used to be

New AI vendors are putting the old guys at risk So PE has disappeared from this segment, and VCs have flocked to hyper-growth AI companies. This may or may not change, but at least don’t live in a dream world where you think the next round is going to come because growth is “pretty good.” It won’t. 8. If You Have Any Doubt About Fundability, Check the Data We literally added a new benchmarking tool at SaaStr.ai. It’s our third tool there. Go to saastr.ai, click “AI VC” at the top. Upload your latest investor update or board deck or VC pitch. We will tell you the exact odds you get funded. The exact odds. And if you don’t like it, don’t shoot the messenger. It’s based on all the recent data from 5,000+ rounds. I talk to way too many founders who think they’re going to get funded in B2B, and they’re not. So just at least find out. We built the tool. It’s benchmarking. It’s cool. 9. AI Is Creating a New Category of “Efficiency Giants” We’re seeing the emergence of what I call “efficiency giants”: companies that can reach $100M+ ARR with teams that would have been laughably small in the SaaS 1.0 era. These companies have: Sub-50 person teams at $50M+ ARR

Gross margins in the 85-90% range

CAC payback under 6 months

Growth rates still above 100% YoY These aren’t just outliers. This is becoming a category. 10. The AI-Native Stack Is Real and Growing Companies are increasingly building on what I call the “AI-native stack”: infrastructure, tooling, and platforms designed specifically for AI workloads and AI-powered applications. This includes: Vector databases (Pinecone, Weaviate)

LLM orchestration layers (LangChain, LlamaIndex)

AI observability and monitoring tools

Model fine-tuning and deployment platforms The total spend on AI-native infrastructure is growing 300%+ YoY, creating a massive new category of B2B software. The Hard Truth About Introducing AI SDRs to Your Team Someone asked me a great question in the live AMA: “How do you start to thoughtfully introduce AI SDRs to the sales team without scaring off the existing SDRs?” I was literally dealing with this yesterday. I was at the company all-hands for a company I invested in called MangoMint (SaaS + AI Agents for salons, spas, and doctor’s offices). Great company, great CEO, great culture. People were just so excited at their all-hands. The CEO asked just one favor of me, “Just do me one favor: don’t scare the SDRs.” He said, “Don’t scare them with all this stuff.” I said, “Okay, I won’t.” But actually, I’d already had lunch before the presentation. I sat down at tables with all the SDRs. I’d already had the conversation with them. They understood that the best have as important a role as ever, and the others don’t. The VP of sales sat down with me afterward and gave the same message. She said, “We’re aggressively all-in on these tools, and we’re growing. We’re growing triple digits at 8 figures in revenue. This is the future. We have to embrace it.” So look, here’s the hard truth: If your SDRs are going to quit because of AI, they’re going to quit anyway. And the tenure of an SDR is very short to begin with. Just be clear: we need everybody who can perform. It was funny. We were sitting there at lunch with the SDRs, and one of them was one of the best ones on Marshall’s team. I’m sitting next to her, and she’s already got her laptop up. She’s scanning a salon that she’s doing outbound to during lunch. She’s literally doing true outbound research during lunch. She’s got a job forever. The SDRs that just want to run random emails and never learn the product? They don’t. I think we’re past the point where you have to worry about scaring the team. Be kind. Make sure everyone who crushes it knows that everyone who is A-tier on your team has a role. That hasn’t changed. It’s even harder to find A-tier folks now. But if folks don’t want to adapt, they won’t have a future. And I think you’re better off being straightforward with them. Just do it. Here’s the other thing: As soon as you actually roll out the tool, someone’s going to quit anyway. This is the story with every company I’ve invested in. Even at SaaStr, on our little team, we rolled out a tool called Momentum (or it might have been from Attention—they’re great too). Even on our little team, the day we rolled it out, someone on our sales team quit. The day we rolled it out. Why? Because now all his actions, all his data were going to show up in real-time in a report and in Salesforce. You couldn’t hide. You couldn’t pretend you did five calls this day when you didn’t. You couldn’t pretend you did the work when you were out at this tool. Somebody quits. And honestly? It’s all for the best. The truth is, it’s all for the best. We’ve got to get out of kumbaya land because this is a new high-growth world. You’ve got to be a part of it. The Real Cost of Implementing AI: What You Actually Need to Budget Another great question: “How much should we be estimating for cost to invest per year in AI to get started?” This is better than it sounds, and the answer is going to surprise you. Let me give you the SaaStr example. We’re tiny. We spend maybe $10,000 a year on Salesforce. Maybe a little more. And the same or a bit more on Marketo, which we essentially use as a CRM for our community (Salesforce is our CRM for sponsors and ‘sales’). I’ve been a Salesforce customer for 20 years. First piece of SaaS I ever purchased for real. I never paid for anything before Salesforce. But here’s the thing: we spent maybe $10K on Salesforce notionally. We spent $500,000 on our AI agents across these 21 agents. $500,000. Think about that ratio for a minute. There are so many learnings in that ratio. It’s why Salesforce has to own Agent Force. They have to win. It’s why HubSpot has to win here. But we are spending far more on agents than we are on CRM. That’s a meta thing to think about. The Real Cost Structure of AI Tools The second thing to think about: these apps that need to be trained with forward-deployed engineers and hands-on work? I don’t think very many of them are less than $30,000 or $50,000 a year. A lot of them actually try to have a price point that’s approaching $100K—like $60K a year base, and then $20K or $30K for the forward-deployed engineer and training. Sometimes they include it, sometimes they charge for it. Whether they do or don’t, it ain’t free to do it right. For me, I would certainly subsidize it if I were a vendor, but it costs that amount. Having a really great technical resource help you train your AI for a couple of weeks? That’s not free. It’s pretty damn expensive. And this relates to the meta issue: You’ve got to invest the time. There’s a reason these apps cost $50K to $100K. They are a lot of money. Be wary of super cheap apps. Be wary. It’s not that we’re not getting there. It’s not that everything isn’t going to get better. But you can’t cut corners on training. If instead of $50K a year, you’re buying a solution that’s $500 a month or $50 a month, I’m not saying it’s not going to work, but you’re going to have to do even more training. You better take on a massive amount of burden to train this app because you’re not getting the benefit of the forward-deployed engineers and all the training, tuning, warming, and everything the vendor does. There’s no shortcut here. There is no shortcut. It is an existential issue. This will change over time, but right now, the agents can’t train the agents themselves the way an FTE does. It’s tough to get away with less than $30K-$50K for any of these tools when a month of training is required—or at least several weeks. What This All Means for You Look, I get it. This is overwhelming. The pace of change is brutal. Every time you think you’ve figured something out, the models get better, the tools evolve, and the playbook shifts. But here’s what you need to take away from all of this: 1. The efficiency advantage is real. AI-native companies are operating with dramatically lower costs and higher margins than classic SaaS ever could. If you’re not thinking about how to capture this advantage, you’re leaving money—and competitive positioning—on the table. 2. You can’t learn by observing. You have to deploy. You have to train. You have to iterate. Reading blog posts and attending webinars isn’t going to cut it. Get in the arena. 3. The funding environment has bifurcated. Hyper-growth AI companies are getting funded at eye-watering valuations. Solid but unspectacular SaaS companies are getting passed over. Know which category you’re in and plan accordingly. 4. Your team structure needs to change. The old GTM playbooks are dying. You don’t need 100 SDRs to scale to $100M anymore. But you do need the right people who can work alongside AI, train it, and amplify their effectiveness with it. 5. Budget for this properly. You’re going to spend more on AI agents than you think. And that’s okay—the ROI is there. But don’t go into this thinking you’re going to deploy enterprise-grade AI solutions for $500/month. You’re not. 6. Speed matters more than ever. The companies that figure this out in the next 12 months are going to have a massive, compounding advantage. The companies that wait are going to find themselves 18-24 months behind, and in this market, that might be fatal. The Bottom Line We’re in the early innings of the biggest shift in B2B software since the move from on-premise to cloud. Maybe bigger. The companies that win are going to be the ones that: Deploy aggressively

Learn constantly
